digest.top_line: ACOSOG Z11 10-yr: OS 86.3% SLNB alone vs 83.6% ALND, LRR 5.3% vs 6.2%; NCCN 2023 talk collates the case for locoregional breast de-escalation.
digest.tldr: No new randomised readouts today, only reviews and practice references. Breast carries the most: an NCCN 2023 talk collating Z11, AMAROS, FAST-Forward and RTOG 1014 behind axillary, PBI and 5-fx de-escalation. CNS pieces target SRS precision: cited 6-mo LC 56% vs 95% with MRI-to-SRS interval ≥14 days; single-isocenter multimet protocols use 0-1 mm PTV margins.

sites.intro: Two SRS technique references: planning-MRI error sources and three centers' single-isocenter multimet protocols. Neither is a prospective outcome study.

studies.name: MRI for brain stereotactic radiotherapy
studies.tldr: 6-mo LC 56% vs 95% with MRI-to-SRS interval ≥14 days; uncorrected gradient distortion would have caused geographic miss in 8 of 28 lesions.
details: 🔍 Narrative review from the Erlangen group, Strahlenther Onkol 2020; companion to the DEGRO/DGMP stereotactic QA papers

details.text: 📊 Planning-MRI error sources and the cited magnitudes

rows: PTV coverage loss up to 34.8% intact mets, up to 4.5% cavities
GTV shift median 1.2 mm, max 3.9 mm; miss in 8 of 28 lesions
Avg 1.6 mm; still 0.8 mm at 12 mm distance

details.text: 📊 Contrast-enhanced T1 sequence comparison (Danieli et al., 16 mets + 38 gliomas)

details: 📐 Consensus tolerance: total MRI distortion <1 mm for brain SRS (2016 MRI-simulation consensus)

details.text: 🔍 Scanner settings the review asks for on a planning MRI
subdetails: Vendor 3D distortion correction; 2D correction leaves through-plane distortion
Patient-specific active shimming
Higher readout bandwidth, accepting SNR loss
Isotropic 3D T1 without slice gaps

details: 📊 Contrast timing: mets <5 mm seen in 40.6% at 10 min vs 75.0% at 20 min (Yuh et al.)
📐 Volumetric error exceeds 10% when the GTV spans <5 slices, relevant for small mets
🔍 Erlangen policy: imaging-to-treatment interval capped at 5 days; repeat MRI at least once in prolonged courses
⚠️ Narrative, not systematic: no search strategy, and cited magnitudes come from small single studies
studies.significance: The fixable error is upstream of the plan: outside diagnostic MRI is often only 2D distortion-corrected, and uncorrected scans shifted GTVs up to 3.9 mm with geographic miss in 8 of 28 lesions, against PTV margins of ≤1 mm. Specifying 3D correction, active shimming, higher bandwidth and isotropic 3D T1 is a protocol decision you can make before contouring.
studies.monday_clinic: In brain mets planned for SRS off an outside diagnostic MRI, the cited data question planning on a scan ≥14 days old or one without 3D distortion correction; it does not inform whole-brain or conventionally fractionated plans.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Narrative review**, single academic group, published alongside the DEGRO/DGMP stereotactic QA editorial and review. No systematic search, no pooled estimate.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Scope is MRI for **target delineation in intracranial SRS/FSRT**, where GTV-to-PTV margins are ≤1 mm. Covers imaging-to-treatment interval, repeat MRI during fractionated courses, positioning, synthetic CT, distortion, sequence choice and contrast timing.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Builds on the **2016 MRI-simulation consensus** (Paulson et al.), which set vendor 3D distortion correction as a minimum and total distortion **<1 mm**. The review adds clinical-impact data on timing, sequence and contrast that the consensus framed as physics requirements.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents brain mets, resection cavities and gliomas planned with stereotactic technique on co-registered MRI. Does not represent whole-brain RT or conventionally fractionated plans with wider margins.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: The T1-SPACE advantage rests on one comparison of 16 mets and 38 gliomas, and none of the sequence or contrast data links delineation to **local control**. Erlangen's 5-day interval cap is institutional policy, not tested.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The case is that MRI error is a **QA problem owned by the radiation oncologist**, not the radiologist. What remains unsettled is whether mask-immobilized MRI or MR-only synthetic CT improves accuracy once current imaging recommendations are already met.

studies.interpretation:
The argument here is that the weakest link in intracranial stereotactic accuracy is often the MRI, not the linac. Linac QA and frameless immobilization get the attention, but the target itself is drawn on a scan that is frequently acquired elsewhere and tuned for diagnosis. The review sets out the ways a diagnostic MRI can mislead a planner: low bandwidth, 2D distortion correction, thick 2D slices with gaps, early post-contrast acquisition and an MPRAGE sequence that under-enhances low-uptake lesions. For a plan with a margin of a millimetre or less, each of these is a geographic-miss risk rather than a cosmetic one.

The strongest clinical anchors are the timing data and the distortion data. Seymour et al. reported 6-month local control of 56% vs 95% when the MRI-to-SRS interval was ≥14 days, and Seibert et al. found that uncorrected images would have produced geographic miss in 8 of 28 lesions. Both are compelling in direction, but a reader should weigh them as signals. The timing comparison is observational and almost certainly confounded: pts who wait longer may differ in disease tempo, referral path or institution. The distortion study is small and dosimetric, estimating what would have happened rather than observing failures. Neither number should be taken as an effect size a protocol change will reproduce.

The sequence comparison is the most practice-relevant claim and also the most fragile. Danieli et al. favoured T1-SPACE on contrast, conspicuity and lesion detection, and MPRAGE missed 15.8% of mets. That is one comparison in 16 mets and 38 gliomas, and larger GTVs on SPACE are not automatically more correct; a bigger contour can mean better boundary depiction or more partial-volume inflation. What would make the recommendation wrong is evidence that the extra SPACE volume is enhancing non-tumour tissue, or that SPACE-drawn targets do not lower marginal failure. The review gives no outcome data either way.

Against the 2016 MRI-simulation consensus, this paper adds little new physics but makes the requirements usable at the console: which DICOM fields reveal whether correction was applied, why higher bandwidth is worth the SNR cost, and why a 3 T scanner with good shimming can outperform an older 1.5 T. That translation is its real contribution. Departments that accept outside MRI by default will see the clearest change, because the review's experience is that most externally acquired scans are only 2D-corrected.

What it leaves open: whether acquiring MRI in the treatment mask helps once 1 mm CT and 1 mm3 3D T1 are standard, whether deep-learning synthetic CT is accurate enough for an MR-only stereotactic workflow, and whether any of the delineation gains translate into fewer local failures. For a radiation oncologist the practical read is a checklist for the planning MRI request, not a new standard backed by outcome data.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Outside diagnostic MRI is often only 2D distortion-corrected, and uncorrected scans shifted GTVs up to 3.9 mm with geographic miss in 8 of 28 lesions, beyond a ≤1 mm PTV margin. Specifying 3D correction, active shimming, higher bandwidth and isotropic 3D T1 on the planning request is the decision this moves.

open_questions: Does mask-immobilized MRI improve registration once 1 mm CT and 3D T1 are used?
Is deep-learning synthetic CT accurate enough for MR-only stereotactic planning?
Does T1-SPACE-based delineation lower marginal failure vs T1-MPRAGE?

studies.name: Single isocenter LINAC radiosurgery for multiple brain metastases: practical considerations
studies.tldr: Three centers' working protocols for single-isocenter multimet SRS: 0-1 mm PTV margin, 6DOF correction, fractionate if largest lesion >2-3 cm or V12 >10 cm3.
details: 🔍 Practical 'how we do it' reference from 3 centers: UAB, Orlando Health (OHCI), UCLA
⚠️ Authors state it is not a consensus guideline; mostly tables, little supporting discussion
⚠️ No outcome data: no local control, radionecrosis, or toxicity results reported
🔍 PTV margin historically 0 mm; typical frameless multimet margin 0 to 1 mm
🔍 6DOF couch used at all 3 centers; can reduce the required PTV margin

subdetails: Fractionate if largest lesion diameter >2 to 3 cm
Fractionate if V12 >10 cm3
3 → 5 fx when OAR constraints can't be met in 3 fx, or by tumor diameter
Fractionated schedules listed: 27 Gy in 3 fractions, 30 Gy in 5 fractions

details: 🔍 Lesions per session generally up to 15, limited by tumor size and intracranial disease volume
⚠️ UAB ignores total V12 in multitarget plans: 10 1-cc targets may be less toxic than 1 10-cc target
⚠️ Distant targets carry rotational-error risk → extra isocenters, tighter rotational tolerance, or larger PTV margin
⚠️ Several authors disclose Varian and Brainlab grants or honoraria, the two platforms described
studies.significance: The portable content is the geometry: PTV margin 0 to 1 mm depends on 6DOF correction, used at all 3 centers, and fractionation starts when the largest lesion exceeds 2-3 cm or V12 >10 cm3. UAB's choice to ignore total V12 across multitarget plans has no necrosis data behind it in this paper.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: A **practical reference, not consensus guidelines**, describing single-isocenter LINAC multimet SRS at UAB, Orlando Health and UCLA. Content is mostly topic-specific tables with references; **no patient outcome data**.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Suitable if metastases are **separated from the optic apparatus** and optic constraints can be met; any other brain location and any histology accepted. SCLC brain metastases historically not universally treated with SRS. Lesions per session **generally up to 15**, shaped by tumor size and intracranial disease volume.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: PTV margin historically 0 mm, typically **0 to 1 mm** for frameless multimet SRS, with a 6DOF couch at all 3 centers. Fractionate when the largest lesion is **>2 to 3 cm or V12 >10 cm3**; listed fractionated schedules are **27 Gy in 3 fractions** and **30 Gy in 5 fractions**, with escalation to 5 fx when OAR constraints fail in 3.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents LINAC programs treating multiple brain metastases with a single isocenter, frameless mask and 6DOF image-guided correction. Does not represent platforms without 6DOF correction or intrafraction monitoring, or dedicated non-LINAC radiosurgery units.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Values in the patient-selection and planning tables are center-specific and vary; the paper does not report the failure or toxicity experience that set each threshold. Applying single-lesion V12 models to multitarget plans is handled differently across centers, and **UAB does not use total V12** at all.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Convergence on margins, 6DOF correction and fractionated schedules gives a defensible middle ground for a new program. Isocenter-to-target distance limits and the multitarget V12 question remain institutional judgement, not evidence.

studies.interpretation:
This paper is best read as a transparency document rather than as evidence. Three experienced centers lay out how they actually run single-isocenter multimet SRS, and the value for a reader lies in seeing where those programs converge and where they quietly diverge. The convergence is reassuring: frameless masks, 6DOF couch correction at every center, PTV margins of 0 to 1 mm, and the same fractionated schedules of 27 Gy in 3 fractions and 30 Gy in 5 fractions. A program building its own protocol can treat that shared ground as the defensible middle.

The divergences teach more. The largest is how normal-brain V12 is handled once targets multiply. Single-lesion V12 models were never built for a plan carrying many small targets, and UAB states openly that it does not apply total V12 to multitarget plans, reasoning that 10 1-cc targets could carry less toxicity than 1 10-cc target. That is a plausible biological argument, but it is an assertion rather than a measured outcome, and the paper offers no radionecrosis data to support or refute it. A reader who adopts that stance is extrapolating from institutional judgement. The same holds for the per-session lesion ceiling (generally up to 15) and for how far a target may sit from isocenter before a second isocenter is added; each center sets these differently, and the paper does not say what failure or toxicity pattern drove the choice.

Methodologically, geometric accuracy is the whole game in single-isocenter delivery. Small rotational errors become larger displacements for lesions far from isocenter, which is why a 0 mm margin rests on 6DOF correction, intrafraction monitoring and tight isocenter QA. The paper describes those safeguards but does not quantify residual targeting error as a function of distance, so the margin recommendation transfers only to a platform with equivalent imaging and couch correction. A center without a 6DOF couch or without intrafraction monitoring should not borrow the 0 mm margin; the authors themselves list a larger PTV margin or tighter rotational tolerance as the alternatives for distant targets.

The disclosures also deserve weight. Several authors report institutional grants, honoraria or royalties from Varian and Brainlab, the two vendors whose integrated systems the paper describes. That does not invalidate a how-we-do-it reference, but it argues for treating the vendor-specific workflow as one validated route rather than the required one.

What the paper does not settle is the clinical question underneath the efficiency gain: whether single-isocenter delivery costs anything in local control or radionecrosis compared with multi-isocenter or dedicated-platform SRS, especially for small targets far from isocenter. That needs outcome data, and none is presented here.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The portable content is the geometry: PTV margin 0 to 1 mm depends on 6DOF correction, used at all 3 centers, and fractionation starts when the largest lesion exceeds 2-3 cm or V12 >10 cm3. UAB's choice to ignore total V12 across multitarget plans has no necrosis data behind it in this paper.

open_questions: Should total V12 constrain multitarget SRS plans?
Safe isocenter-to-target distance for single-isocenter plans
Necrosis and local control vs multi-isocenter delivery

sites.intro: NMSC hypofractionation: a single-author POV on short-course schedules by age and PS, plus an n=1 HDR surface mould eyelid case.

studies.name: HDR surface mould brachytherapy for eyelid carcinoma
studies.tldr: Disease-free at 6 mo with only mild dry eye after 52 Gy/13 fx HDR surface mould to an excised upper-eyelid sebaceous carcinoma, n=1.
details: 🔍 Single-pt case report: step-by-step technique plus 9 consecutive weekly post-treatment reviews
🔍 54F, sebaceous carcinoma R upper eyelid near lateral canthus, 0.8 × 0.5 cm
🔍 Excisional biopsy with margin status not reported; MRI showed no residual disease, no nodes

subdetails: 52 Gy/13 fx, 4 Gy/fx BID, 6 h apart
Ir-192 via Flexitron afterloader
EQD2 60.67 Gy, judged equivalent to 60 Gy LDR
CTV = scar (copper wire on CT) + 1 cm margin, no PTV; CTV 0.71 mL
5-mm lead shield wrapped in wax placed under the lid each fraction
Dummy wax mould used at CT to avoid lead artifact
IPSA inverse planning, Oncentra Brachy 4.6.0
D90 at least 90% of Rx; DNR 0.26 vs limit < 0.36

details: 📊 Disease-free at 6 mo post-treatment
📊 No acute side effects; mild dry eye the only toxicity
⚠️ No residual disease at RT: tumor control here is adjuvant, not definitive
⚠️ OAR doses (lens, lacrimal, anterior chamber) given only in Fig 3D, not in source text
⚠️ 6-mo f/u too short to capture cataract or late ocular surface effects
🔗 Surgery (WLE or Mohs) is the stated standard; GEC-ESTRO favors brachy over EBRT for small skin targets

verdict.rationale: Single-patient case report with 6-mo follow-up; a technique description, not efficacy evidence. No comparator against surgery or electrons.
verdict.audience: Excised upper-eyelid sebaceous carcinoma, margins unknown, no MRI residual

studies.significance: What transfers is the setup, not the outcome: a 5-mm wax-wrapped lead shield under the lid, a dummy wax mould at CT to avoid lead artifact, CTV as scar wire + 1 cm with no PTV, and plan acceptance by D90 and DNR 0.26. The tumor was already excised with no MRI residual, so this informs adjuvant scar treatment, not gross disease.
studies.monday_clinic: In a pt with a small excised eyelid carcinoma, margins unreported and no residual on MRI, who declines further surgery or an interstitial implant, this supports surface mould HDR as a feasible noninvasive adjuvant option; it does not extend to gross or recurrent eyelid tumors.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Single-patient case report** describing the surface mould HDR workflow step by step, followed by **weekly review for 9 consecutive weeks**. Last reported status is at 6 mo post-treatment.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: 54-year-old woman with a 0.8 × 0.5 cm **sebaceous carcinoma of the right upper eyelid** near the lateral canthus, diagnosed on excisional biopsy with **margin status not reported**. MRI of the face and neck showed **no residual disease** and no lymphadenopathy. She declined surgery and any invasive procedure.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **52 Gy/13 fx at 4 Gy/fx BID, 6 h apart**, Ir-192 on a Flexitron afterloader, chosen as LQ-equivalent (EQD2 60.67 Gy) to 60 Gy LDR. **CTV = scar + 1 cm, no PTV** (0.71 mL), planned with IPSA; a 5-mm wax-wrapped lead shield sat under the lid each fraction. Coverage met **D90 at least 90% of Rx** with **DNR 0.26** (limit < 0.36).

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: **Disease-free at 6 mo** post-treatment.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: **No acute side effects**; **mild dry eye** the only reported toxicity. OAR doses are stated as within tolerance but the values sit in a figure table, not the source text.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Surgery, by wide local excision or Mohs, is the stated standard for eyelid carcinoma. GEC-ESTRO favors brachytherapy over external beam for small skin targets, and the authors chose surface mould over electrons for its sharper fall-off. The brachytherapy literature they cite has no randomized or cohort data, only small series that are mostly BCC.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents a small, already-excised eyelid carcinoma with unreported margins and no residual disease on MRI. Does not represent gross, recurrent, or nodal eyelid disease, where tumor control has not been tested here.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: With no residual tumor at RT, the outcome reflects adjuvant scar treatment and says nothing about controlling gross disease. The α/β behind the EQD2 equivalence is not stated in the source text, and lens and lacrimal doses cannot be checked from the text.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The paper is useful as a **reproducible workflow** for a department with an HDR afterloader and no interstitial eyelid experience. It does not settle late ocular toxicity, the best fractionation, or how the approach compares with surgery for cosmesis or control.

studies.interpretation:
This is a technique note with one patient attached, and its value is in the procedure rather than the outcome. The patient had an excisional biopsy with unreported margins and then an MRI showing no residual disease, so the brachytherapy was in effect adjuvant treatment to a scar volume. Being disease-free at 6 months in that setting says very little about whether surface mould HDR can control gross eyelid tumor. Gross disease is the question that would place this technique against Mohs or wide excision, and the paper's organ-preservation framing claims more than a single adjuvant course can support.

The comparative base is thin, and the authors say so: they describe no randomized trials or cohort studies of eyelid brachytherapy, and only one systematic review, which also lacked them. The earlier surface mould series in their comparison table are small and mostly basal cell carcinoma. Sebaceous histology appears in only a handful of cases, so extending these results to sebaceous carcinoma rests largely on this one patient. A reader should take the comparison table as proof that the technique has been done before, not as pooled efficacy data.

The dosimetric reasoning deserves a closer look. The prescription was chosen as LQ-equivalent to 60 Gy LDR, with an EQD2 of 60.67 Gy. The α/β behind that figure is not given in the source text. That matters because the structures that limit this treatment, the lens and lacrimal apparatus beneath the lid, are late-responding, and an equivalence tuned to tumor does not carry over to them. Twice-daily fractions 6 hours apart allow for sublethal damage repair but are a practical compromise. The authors report OAR doses as within tolerance, but the numbers sit in a figure, so a reader cannot check lens dose against their own constraints. The coverage criteria (D90 against prescription, DNR under the stated limit) are standard and were met.

What carries over is the workflow. The wax-wrapped lead shield limits backscatter and contact with the globe, the dummy wax mould removes lead artifact from the planning CT, the copper wire marks the scar, and no PTV is added beyond the CTV. A department with an HDR afterloader could adopt this setup for a small post-excision eyelid target in a patient who refuses more surgery or an implant. The paper also explains why the tumor board preferred this over electrons: sharper dose fall-off and shallower penetration.

The main way this could prove wrong is late effects. Cataract, worsening dry eye and lid changes typically appear well after 6 months, and the mild dry eye already reported may be an early sign of them. A marginal recurrence outside a scar-plus-1 cm CTV would challenge the target definition. Neither question can be answered at this follow-up.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: What transfers is the setup: a wax-wrapped 5-mm lead shield under the lid, a dummy wax mould at CT, and CTV as scar + 1 cm with no PTV, accepted on D90 and DNR 0.26. Because the tumor was excised with no MRI residual, this informs adjuvant scar treatment, not definitive treatment of gross eyelid disease.

open_questions: Late lens and lacrimal toxicity beyond 6 mo
Control of gross eyelid sebaceous carcinoma with surface mould HDR
Optimal HDR fractionation for eyelid skin cancers

studies.name: Hypofractionated RT in non-melanoma skin cancer, post-COVID-19
studies.tldr: Single-author POV argues for ≤15 fx in most NMSC and 1–4 fx as default for ≥80 or ECOG 2/3; hypofractionated LC cited at 90–100%.
details: 🔍 Point-of-view article (JMIRO 2020), single author; no new outcome data
📊 Cited LC with definitive RT, any technique: >90–95%
📊 Cited LC with hypofractionated RT in NMSC: 90–100%
🔗 Cited systematic review: 40 publications, over 12 000 NMSC, mean dose 38 Gy, 8 Gy/fx, 3x/week
🔗 RCR (UK) suggested trimming: 40 Gy/8 fx instead of 10; 50 Gy/15 fx instead of 55 Gy/20 fx

details.text: 💊 Suggested schedules, localised BCC, by age/PS
💊 Suggested schedules, localised SCC, by age/PS

details: ⚠️ Table rows rebuilt from a scrambled PDF text layer; check cell placement against the original Table 1
❓ Footnote: consider adjuvant RT vs observation in most BCCs and low-risk SCCs

studies.significance: The real change is the frailty-stratified grid, not a uniform cut in fraction count: ≥80 or ECOG 2/3 drops to 15–28 Gy in 1–4 fx, and ECOG 3/4 adjuvant cases go to no RT. Longer 45–50 Gy in 15–20 fx is kept only for perioral/orbital sites in pts <70, so the decision this moves is fraction count by frailty, with omission of adjuvant RT in most BCC and low-risk SCC.
studies.monday_clinic: In pts ≥80 or ECOG 2/3 with localised BCC or SCC, this supports 1–4 fraction courses over protracted schedules; it does not extend to PNI fields over neural structures or high-risk lower lip SCC, where 20 or 25 fractions may still be justified.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Point-of-view article**, single author, Journal of Medical Imaging and Radiation Oncology 2020. Proposes suggested schedules (Table 1); reports **no new outcome data**.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Conventional pts <70: **55–50 Gy in 2–2.5 Gy** fx. Ages 70–80: **40–45 Gy in 10–15 fx**. Proposed default for ≥80 or ECOG 2/3: **15–28 Gy in 1–4 fx**, delivered second daily or weekly. Illustrated case: 28 Gy in 4 fx twice weekly, orthovoltage.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: More aggressive than the RCR (UK) guidance cited, which trimmed **40 Gy/8 fx instead of 10** and **50 Gy/15 fx instead of 55 Gy/20**. Cites a systematic review of 40 publications (over 12 000 NMSC) centred on **8 Gy/fx, 3x/week**.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents localised BCC and SCC of skin in the definitive or adjuvant setting, stratified by age and ECOG. Does not represent PNI cases needing larger fields over neural structures or high-risk lower lip SCC treated for oral competence.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Schedule ranges are wide within each cell (e.g. 30–45 Gy in 5–15 fx), so the grid sets a fraction-count ceiling, not a validated dose. Late cosmesis is traded explicitly: the illustrated case shows **in-field hypopigmentation and epidermal atrophy** at 6 months.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The pandemic is the trigger, but the claim is that hypofractionation **should not be seen as less optimal treatment**. The adjuvant observation footnote is an **omission** argument and rests on thinner data than the fractionation argument.

studies.interpretation:
The argument is less about COVID-19 than about a fractionation habit the evidence never required. Veness's point is that long courses for NMSC, typically 55–50 Gy in 2–2.5 Gy fractions for pts under 70, persist mainly to limit late cutaneous change. The literature he cites reports local control of 90–100% with hypofractionated schedules, and a systematic review of 40 publications covering over 12 000 lesions centred on 8 Gy fractions delivered 3 times per week. The pandemic supplies the pressure. The proposal is that resource scarcity should make shorter schedules the default rather than the exception.

Against the UK guidance cited in the piece, the proposal goes further. The Royal College of Radiologists suggested modest trims (40 Gy in 8 fractions rather than 10, 50 Gy in 15 rather than 55 Gy in 20). Veness instead stratifies by age and ECOG and moves the oldest and frailest group to 15–28 Gy in 1–4 fractions, with a single 15–18 Gy fraction or no RT at the far end. That is a different kind of change: schedules reallocated by frailty and competing mortality, rather than one uniform reduction applied to everyone.

Confidence should match the evidence base, which the author himself calls low quality: mostly observational cohorts, very few randomised studies, and wide heterogeneity in lesions, technique (external beam vs brachytherapy) and dose. High local control in pooled observational series partly reflects who gets offered hypofractionation, often small, superficial lesions in elderly pts whose competing mortality shortens the window for late recurrence or late toxicity to appear. The illustrated case (an 88-year-old with recurrent SCC and a positive deep margin, treated with 28 Gy in 4 fractions) shows feasibility and a clean 6-month result. It does not show durability.

For a radiation oncologist, the trade-off that matters is late cosmesis in younger pts with long life expectancy. Hypopigmentation and epidermal atrophy are visible even in the showcase case, and the grid keeps 45–50 Gy in 15–20 fractions for perioral and orbital sites in pts under 70. The stated exceptions, PNI fields over neural structures and high-risk lower lip SCC where oral competence is the goal, are where 20 or 25 fractions stay justified. The piece does not argue against them.

The more provocative content is the adjuvant footnote, which invites observation in most BCCs and low-risk SCCs. That is an omission decision, not a fractionation one, and the cited data say even less about it. Two things would undercut the argument: higher late recurrence, or unacceptable late toxicity, with 1–4 fraction schedules in fit pts with long life expectancy. The observational literature it rests on was not built to detect either.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The grid sorts fraction count by frailty: ≥80 or ECOG 2/3 goes to 15–28 Gy in 1–4 fx, and protracted 45–50 Gy in 15–20 fx is kept only for perioral/orbital sites in pts <70. It also pushes observation over adjuvant RT for most BCC and low-risk SCC.

open_questions: Adjuvant RT vs observation in most BCC and low-risk SCC
Late cosmesis with 1–4 fraction schedules in younger pts
Randomised comparison of fractionation schedules in NMSC

studies.significance: The nodal pCR cohort supporting ALND omission after NAC delivered nodal RT to 78% (SLNB) and 85% (TAD), so it does not license dropping RNI too. On the breast side, NCCN 2023 now names moderately HF PBI, backed by less Grade II/III induration with PBI 40 Gy/15 fx in the Danish trial.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: NCCN 2023 Breast Cancer Congress session with **SABCS 2022 updates**, split into a surgical half and a radiation half. Evidence ranges from **phase 3 non-inferiority trials** (Z11, AMAROS, IMPORT LOW, Danish PBI) to single-arm phase 2 data and retrospective series, each mapped to an NCCN guideline change.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Z11 enrolled 891 pts: **cT1-2, no palpable adenopathy, 1-2 positive SLNs**, lumpectomy with WBRT planned; mastectomy and **third-field (nodal) irradiation excluded**. AMAROS allowed lumpectomy or mastectomy in T1-2 unifocal disease.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: PBI schedules shown: **30 Gy QOD x 5** IMRT (Florence), **40 Gy/15** (IMPORT LOW, Danish), and **1.5 Gy BID to 45 Gy** for re-irradiation (RTOG 1014). Weekly setup imaging is the NCCN minimum, with daily imaging not recommended as standard; DIBH is established for left-sided cases.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Z11 and AMAROS together frame axillary management after a positive SLN: dissection omitted with breast RT, or replaced by axillary RT. NCCN endorsed FAST in 2021 and **allowed FAST-Forward in 2022**, and broadened APBI to **PBI/APBI including moderately HF regimens** in 2023.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents cT1-2 breast cancer treated with breast conservation, including 1-2 positive SLNs, low-risk PBI candidates and selected isolated IBTR. Does not represent pts with residual nodal disease after NAC or the decision to omit regional nodal RT after nodal pCR.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Several results slides (the SABCS nodal pCR outcomes, the Yale right-sided DIBH dosimetry) carry **no extractable numbers** in the source. The hypofractionated RNI section is truncated mid-table.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The surgical de-escalation steps each lean on RT doing more of the regional work, which the talk states implicitly rather than testing. The RT half settles that **schedule, not the PBI concept**, drove earlier cosmetic penalties, but leaves the optimal EBRT-PBI technique for long-term cosmesis open, as NCCN itself says.

studies.interpretation:
The talk is most useful for how it stacks de-escalation steps that were tested separately, not for any one result. The axillary argument rests on two randomized non-inferiority trials that asked different questions. Z11 asked whether completion dissection adds anything when the breast receives tangential RT and the nodes receive no deliberate field. AMAROS asked whether axillary RT can replace dissection. Read together, they imply that residual nodal disease after a positive SLN is controlled by systemic therapy plus whatever RT reaches the low axilla, not by further surgery. The detail that 27% of ALND pts had additional positive nodes, while locoregional recurrence stayed at 6.2% vs 5.3%, is the strongest version of that argument, and it is also where an RT reader should slow down: Z11 excluded third-field nodal irradiation by design, yet the talk never asks how much axilla the tangents covered.

The post-NAC material pushes the same logic into territory where RT carries more of the load. The SABCS 2022 cohort omitting ALND after nodal pCR delivered nodal RT to 78% after SLNB and 85% after TAD, so whatever regional control it reports belongs partly to RT. That series supports dropping the dissection; it says nothing about dropping RNI, which is the question NSABP B-51 was designed to answer. The staging data (TAD FNR 2.0% vs 10.1% for SLNB alone) make the surgical omission defensible, but a lower FNR is a staging claim, not an outcome.

On breast RT, the meta-analysis is the hinge. The pooled RR of 1.72 reflects technique heterogeneity; restricted to 3D-planned EBRT and brachytherapy, IBTR was 3.3% vs 2.6% with RR 1.25 and P = .05, and the slide frames the absolute gap as under 1%. That is reassuring for the population enrolled (mostly T1N0, grade 1 or 2) and silent beyond it. The schedule data explain the cosmesis story better than the technique data do: trials reporting worse toxicity used 3.85 Gy BID to 38.5 Gy, while Florence (30 Gy QOD x 5) showed no cosmetic difference and the Danish trial found less Grade II/III induration with PBI at 40 Gy/15. FAST-Forward adds a caution in the other direction: 26 Gy matched 40 Gy/15 on most effects but not on whole-breast induration and edema.

The repeat-BCT and multifocal sections are the thinnest evidence presented. RTOG 1014 is single-arm with 58 evaluable pts and strict eligibility (<3cm, unifocal, >1 yr to IBTR), so its 5.2% second-IBTR rate describes a selected group. In the multifocal series, LR was 3/15 without MRI against 3/189 with MRI, which suggests imaging selection may be doing much of the work. What would make the overall framework wrong is longer follow-up showing regional failures concentrated in pts who skipped both dissection and nodal RT, a combination none of the presented data tested.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: ALND omission after nodal pCR rests on a cohort where 78% (SLNB) and 85% (TAD) received nodal RT, so the RNI decision stays open. For the breast, NCCN 2023 adds moderately HF PBI, and the Danish trial showed less Grade II/III induration with PBI 40 Gy/15.
significance_by_specialty.surgonc: Z11 at 10 yrs held OS 83.6% vs 86.3% without completion ALND despite 27% additional positive nodes in the ALND arm. After NAC, TAD cut FNR to 2.0% vs 10.1% for SLNB alone, the staging step that supports omitting dissection after nodal pCR.

presentation.summary: The speakers argued that locoregional therapy for non-metastatic breast cancer is moving toward personalized de-escalation across surgery and RT. On the surgical side, ACOSOG Z11 and AMAROS anchor omission of completion ALND for 1-2 positive SLNs, while dual tracer mapping, clipped-node retrieval and TAD lower the false-negative rate of axillary staging after NAC. Breast conservation for 2 or 3 ipsilateral foci was presented as acceptable on prospective SABCS 2022 data. On the RT side, moderately hypofractionated PBI, FAST and FAST-Forward schedules, and repeat BCT with PBI for selected IBTR were framed against the corresponding NCCN guideline changes.
critique: Z11 excluded third-field nodal RT, and the talk does not address incidental axillary dose from tangents, so how much breast RT substituted for dissection is left unexamined.
The SABCS nodal pCR cohort gave nodal RT to 78% after SLNB and 85% after TAD; it supports omitting dissection, not omitting regional RT, and it is non-randomized.
The PBI meta-analysis pooled heterogeneous techniques in mostly T1N0 grade 1 or 2 pts, and the restricted comparison sat at P = .05, so equivalence outside that population remains unproven.
Hypofractionated RNI rests on historic plexopathy series, British Columbia PMRT and START, where only 14% received RNI; no randomized nodal data for a 5-fraction schedule are shown.

papers.title: Practical Considerations for Single Isocenter LINAC Radiosurgery of Multiple Brain Metastases
Magnetic resonance imaging for brain stereotactic radiotherapy
papers.abstract: Abstract Due to its superior soft tissue contrast, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is essential for many radiotherapy treatment indications. This is especially true for treatment planning in intracranial tumors, where MRI has a long-standing history for target delineation in clinical practice. Despite its routine use, care has to be taken when selecting and acquiring MRI studies for the purpose of radiotherapy treatment planning. Requirements on MRI are particularly demanding for intracranial stereotactic radiotherapy, where accurate imaging has a critical role in treatment success. However, MR images acquired for routine radiological assessment are frequently unsuitable for high-precision stereotactic radiotherapy as the requirements for imaging are significantly different for radiotherapy planning and diagnostic radiology. To assure that optimal imaging is used for treatment planning, the radiation oncologist needs proper knowledge of the most important requirements concerning the use of MRI in brain stereotactic radiotherapy. In the present review, we summarize and discuss the most relevant issues when using MR images for target volume delineation in intracranial stereotactic radiotherapy.

papers.title: Implementing high-dose rate surface mould brachytherapy for carcinoma of eyelid: a practical approach and weekly review
papers.abstract: Surface mould brachytherapy is a conformal radiotherapy technique that can deliver high dose to the target while sparing nearby normal structures, Here, we aim to describe the procedurals details for high-dose rate (HDR) surface mould brachytherapy in sebaceous carcinoma of eyelid in a 54-year old lady. She was hesitant for surgery and any form of invasive intervention like interstitial brachytherapy. So, she was treated with surface mould HDR brachytherapy to a total dose of 52 Gy in 13 fractions at a dose of 4 Gy per fraction delivered twice daily using Iridium-192 isotope with no acute side effects. She was evaluated on a weekly basis for any radiation side effects and now she is disease-free for 6 months post-treatment with only mild dry eye. A detailed step-by-step procedure of surface mould technique, simulation procedure, dose prescription, planning, plan evaluation and treatment has been described in this paper. Surface mould HDR brachytherapy can be safely used as organ preserving modality of treatment for eyelid carcinoma.
